reference.source: Rutherford's Vascular Surgery / Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine
clinicalPearls: Represents atherosclerotic inflow disease of the distal aorta and iliac arteries and often coexists with more distal (femoropopliteal) disease
The classic Leriche triad comprises buttock, hip, and thigh claudication, diminished or absent femoral pulses, and erectile dysfunction in men
Because obstruction is proximal, claudication is typically felt in the buttocks and thighs rather than the calves alone
Well-developed collateral pathways can maintain limb viability despite extensive occlusion, so rest pain is less common than in multilevel disease
Duplex ultrasound, CT angiography, or MR angiography define the pattern and length of disease to guide endovascular versus open reconstruction
Focal iliac stenoses are well suited to endovascular treatment, while extensive aortoiliac occlusion may require aortobifemoral bypass or extra-anatomic reconstruction
Risk-factor modification, particularly smoking cessation, antiplatelet therapy, and statins, underpins all management
Presence of aortoiliac disease signals widespread atherosclerosis with a high burden of coronary and cerebrovascular risk
reference.pathophysiology: Aortoiliac occlusive disease is caused by progressive atherosclerotic plaque within the infrarenal aorta and common and external iliac arteries, reducing arterial inflow to the pelvis and lower limbs. Because the obstruction is proximal, symptoms involve the buttocks and thighs and, in men, erectile function through compromise of the internal iliac supply. Gradual stenosis stimulates collateral development via lumbar, mesenteric, and pelvic pathways, which can preserve limb perfusion. When inflow disease coexists with infrainguinal disease (multilevel disease), the additive resistance more readily precipitates rest pain and tissue loss.
additionalInvestigations: Ankle-brachial index with segmental pressures to localise the level of disease
Arterial duplex ultrasound of the aortoiliac and femoral segments
CT or MR angiography, or catheter angiography, for reconstructive planning
Cardiovascular risk assessment including lipids, glucose, and smoking status
Cardiac and functional assessment before major open reconstruction
redFlags: Rest pain, ulceration, or gangrene indicating limb-threatening ischaemia and urgent vascular referral
Acute-on-chronic occlusion with sudden severe limb ischaemia, a limb-threatening emergency
Rapidly progressive symptoms or tissue loss
Concurrent features of severe cardiovascular disease
reference.prognosis: Isolated aortoiliac disease with good collateral flow often has a favourable limb outlook, and revascularisation, whether endovascular or bypass, provides durable symptom relief in appropriately selected patients. Overall survival is chiefly limited by concurrent coronary and cerebrovascular atherosclerosis.
pitfalls: Misattributing buttock and thigh claudication to hip or spinal disease
Overlooking coexisting infrainguinal disease that limits the benefit of inflow correction alone
Underestimating cardiovascular risk and omitting systemic prevention
Failing to recognise Leriche syndrome in men presenting with erectile dysfunction and claudication
